summary.text: Introduce auxiliary recurrences \(d_0=1,d_1=7,d_{n+2}=-d_{n+1}-4d_n\) and \(e_0=1,e_1=-11,e_{n+2}=-7e_{n+1}-16e_n\); a quadratic invariant relating \(e_n,d_n,d_{n+1}\) yields the identities needed to match the original fourth-order recurrence. Simultaneous induction then gives \(a_{2n}=-16^n e_n\) and \(a_{2n+1}=4\cdot16^n d_n^2=(2\cdot4^n d_n)^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that every term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square by obtaining an explicit square representation.

Introduce two auxiliary integer sequences \((d_n)\) and \((e_n)\) by
\[
d_0=1,\qquad d_1=7,\qquad d_{n+2}=-d_{n+1}-4d_n,
\tag{2}
\]
and
\[
e_0=1,\qquad e_1=-11,\qquad e_{n+2}=-7e_{n+1}-16e_n.
\tag{3}
\]
The key point is that the two auxiliary sequences are connected by a quadratic invariant.

### 1. A quadratic relation between \(d_n\) and \(e_n\)

We claim that, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
60e_n=11d_n^2+14d_nd_{n+1}-d_{n+1}^2.
\tag{4}
\]

For \(n=0\), the right-hand side is
\[
11\cdot 1^2+14\cdot 1\cdot 7-7^2=11+98-49=60=60e_0.
\]
For \(n=1\), recurrence (2) gives
\[
d_2=-d_1-4d_0=-7-4=-11.
\]
Consequently,
\[
11d_1^2+14d_1d_2-d_2^2
=11\cdot49+14\cdot7\cdot(-11)-121
=539-1078-121=-660=60e_1.
\]

It remains to prove the induction step. It is useful to write
\[
Q(u,v)=11u^2+14uv-v^2.
\]
Suppose (4) is known at indices \(k\) and \(k+1\). Put
\[
x=d_k,\qquad y=d_{k+1},\qquad z=d_{k+2},\qquad w=d_{k+3}.
\]
By (2),
\[
z=-y-4x,
\qquad
w=-z-4y=4x-3y.
\tag{5}
\]
The two induction hypotheses say
\[
60e_k=Q(x,y),\qquad 60e_{k+1}=Q(y,z).
\]
Using recurrence (3),
\[
60e_{k+2}=-7Q(y,z)-16Q(x,y).
\tag{6}
\]
Direct substitution from (5) gives
\[
Q(x,y)=11x^2+14xy-y^2,
\]
\[
Q(y,z)=-16x^2-64xy-4y^2,
\]
and
\[
Q(z,w)=-64x^2+224xy+44y^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
-7Q(y,z)-16Q(x,y)
=-64x^2+224xy+44y^2
=Q(z,w).
\]
Together with (6), this proves
\[
60e_{k+2}=Q(d_{k+2},d_{k+3}),
\]
which is (4) at index \(k+2\). Thus (4) holds for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

### 2. Two transition identities

We next derive two identities that will match the fourth-order recurrence for \(a_n\). For every \(n\ge 0\), we claim
\[
e_{n+2}=d_{n+1}^2-4d_n^2+16e_n,
\tag{7}
\]
and
\[
d_{n+2}^2=e_{n+2}-4e_{n+1}+16d_n^2.
\tag{8}
\]

Fix \(n\) and again put
\[
x=d_n,\qquad y=d_{n+1},\qquad z=d_{n+2}=-y-4x,
\qquad w=d_{n+3}=4x-3y.
\]
By (4),
\[
60e_n=Q(x,y),\qquad
60e_{n+1}=Q(y,z),\qquad
60e_{n+2}=Q(z,w).
\tag{9}
\]
The expansions already used above are
\[
Q(x,y)=11x^2+14xy-y^2,
\]
\[
Q(y,z)=-16x^2-64xy-4y^2,
\]
\[
Q(z,w)=-64x^2+224xy+44y^2.
\tag{10}
\]
Now
\[
\begin{aligned}
60\bigl(y^2-4x^2+16e_n\bigr)
&=60y^2-240x^2+16Q(x,y)\\
&=60y^2-240x^2
  +176x^2+224xy-16y^2\\
&=-64x^2+224xy+44y^2\\
&=Q(z,w)\\
&=60e_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since these are integer equalities, cancellation of the nonzero factor \(60\) proves (7).

Similarly, using (9) and (10),
\[
\begin{aligned}
60\bigl(e_{n+2}-4e_{n+1}+16x^2\bigr)
&=Q(z,w)-4Q(y,z)+960x^2\\
&=960x^2+480xy+60y^2\\
&=60(16x^2+8xy+y^2)\\
&=60(4x+y)^2\\
&=60z^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(z=-4x-y\). Cancelling \(60\) proves (8).

### 3. Formulas for the even and odd subsequences of \(a_n\)

We now prove simultaneously that, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{2n}=-16^n e_n
\tag{11}
\]
and
\[
a_{2n+1}=4\cdot16^n d_n^2.
\tag{12}
\]

For \(n=0\), these equations read
\[
a_0=-e_0=-1,
\qquad
a_1=4d_0^2=4,
\]
which agree with the initial values.

For \(n=1\), they read
\[
a_2=-16e_1=-16(-11)=176
\]
and
\[
a_3=4\cdot16\cdot d_1^2
=64\cdot49=3136,
\]
again exactly the prescribed initial values.

Suppose now that both (11) and (12) are known at indices \(k\) and \(k+1\). We prove both formulas at index \(k+2\).

First apply recurrence (1) with \(r=2k\):
\[
a_{2k+4}=-4a_{2k+3}+256a_{2k+1}+4096a_{2k}.
\]
The induction hypotheses give
\[
a_{2k+3}=4\cdot16^{k+1}d_{k+1}^2,
\quad
a_{2k+1}=4\cdot16^k d_k^2,
\quad
a_{2k}=-16^k e_k.
\]
Substitution and factoring out \(16^k\) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2k+4}
&=-4\bigl(4\cdot16^{k+1}d_{k+1}^2\bigr)
 +256\bigl(4\cdot16^kd_k^2\bigr)
 -4096\cdot16^ke_k\\
&=16^k\bigl(-256d_{k+1}^2+1024d_k^2-4096e_k\bigr)\\
&=-256\cdot16^k
   \bigl(d_{k+1}^2-4d_k^2+16e_k\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
By identity (7), the expression in parentheses is \(e_{k+2}\). Hence
\[
a_{2k+4}=-256\cdot16^k e_{k+2}
=-16^{k+2}e_{k+2}.
\]
Since \(2k+4=2(k+2)\), this proves (11) at \(k+2\).

We may now use this newly established even-index formula to obtain the following odd-index term. Applying (1) with \(r=2k+1\) gives
\[
a_{2k+5}=-4a_{2k+4}+256a_{2k+2}+4096a_{2k+1}.
\]
We have just proved
\[
a_{2k+4}=-16^{k+2}e_{k+2},
\]
while the induction hypotheses give
\[
a_{2k+2}=-16^{k+1}e_{k+1},
\qquad
a_{2k+1}=4\cdot16^kd_k^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2k+5}
&=4\cdot16^{k+2}e_{k+2}
  -256\cdot16^{k+1}e_{k+1}
  +16384\cdot16^kd_k^2\\
&=4\cdot16^{k+2}
  \bigl(e_{k+2}-4e_{k+1}+16d_k^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Identity (8) identifies the expression in parentheses with \(d_{k+2}^2\). Therefore
\[
a_{2k+5}=4\cdot16^{k+2}d_{k+2}^2.
\]
Since \(2k+5=2(k+2)+1\), this is (12) at index \(k+2\). The two base cases and this two-step induction prove (11) and (12) for all \(n\ge 0\).

### 4. The odd terms are squares

From (12), for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{2n+1}=4\cdot16^n d_n^2.
\]
Since \(16^n=(4^n)^2\), this becomes
\[
a_{2n+1}
=2^2(4^n)^2d_n^2
=\bigl(2\cdot4^n d_n\bigr)^2.
\]
The quantity \(2\cdot4^n d_n\) is an integer. Hence \(a_{2n+1}\) is a perfect square for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
